title: King Nriga's cow
hook: a king famous for giving away cows is found as a lizard in a well, and tells Krishna why
carry: good and bad both bind; offer the act
tomorrow: a sage, a fish, and an old desire

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nandi and Nahusha, one raised by devotion, one dropped by pride. As you act, so you become.

In the Bhagavata Purana, some of Krishna's sons are out playing near Dvaraka and go looking for water. In a dry well they find a lizard, enormous, the size of a hill. They try ropes, they try leather straps; they can't lift it. So they run for their father. Krishna reaches down with his left hand and lifts it out, and at his touch the lizard becomes a shining man. Who are you? Krishna asks, though he knows. And the man says: I was a king. Nriga. Famous for giving.
screen: `A LIZARD THE SIZE OF A HILL.` → `KRISHNA LIFTS IT OUT.` → `I WAS A KING.`

segments.voice: Nriga had given away cows beyond counting, he says, as many as grains of sand, as stars. Then one day a cow he'd already given to one brahmin strayed back into his herd, and without knowing it, he gave her again, to another. The first man saw his cow being led away. The two argued it out before the king, and Nriga offered each a hundred thousand cows to let the other keep her. Both refused, and left angry. When Nriga died, Yama, judge of the dead, asked him: your good first, or your fault? He chose the fault first, and became the lizard in the well. Here's the teaching, and it surprises people. In Hindu thought, good karma doesn't cancel bad karma like a bank balance. Both ripen. Nriga got both. That's why, for Patanjali, even bright karma isn't the goal. Sutra 4.7: the action of the yogi is neither white nor black; for everyone else it's of three kinds, black, white and mixed. All three leave seeds. The fourth kind leaves none, because it's done without craving its fruit. The Gita names the way: whatever you do, eat, offer or give, do it as an offering to me, and you'll be freed from the bonds of good and bad results alike. So many Hindus finish a meal, or a day's work, with a quiet line: Krishnarpanam astu. Let this be offered to Krishna. The act still happens. The cows still get given. Nobody stands there waiting for the harvest.
screen: `ONE COW, GIVEN TWICE.` · `YOUR GOOD FIRST, OR YOUR FAULT?` · `BOTH RIPEN.` · `4.7: NEITHER WHITE NOR BLACK.` · `KRISHNARPANAM ASTU.` · then, large: `GOOD AND BAD BOTH BIND; OFFER THE ACT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing you did recently, and notice if anything is stuck to it: a wish to be thanked, to be seen as good, to have it count. If you pray, offer it silently: Krishnarpanam astu, or in your own words, this is yours. If you don't, set the wish down and let the good act stand on its own. It happened, and it was good.
Ashukla-akrishna, neither white nor black. The yogi's karma, done fully and offered, free of its fruit, so it plants no seed.
Your line: good and bad both bind; offer the act. Krishnarpanam astu. Until tomorrow, when an old desire wakes.

howItsDone: Many Hindus offer meals and work to God with words like Krishnarpanam astu, following the Gita's teaching (9.27–28) that action offered to God frees one from the bonds of good and bad results; teachers of the Yoga Sutras read 4.7 alongside it.

chat.meaning: Nriga's countless gifts didn't cancel his one mistake: both ripened. Patanjali calls the yogi's action neither white nor black, and the Gita says offered action frees you from both.
